That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.The company has yet to turn a profit. national.summary: Maurene Comey was abruptly fired in July 2025 from her job as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. She sued the DOJ over her firing, claiming it was unlawful.

The judge retroactively reinstated Comey to her role as a federal prosecutor and ordered the Trump administration to provide her back pay from the date of her firing in July 2025 through Dec. 20, when she accepted a different job.Comey's lawsuit was one of several filed by former government employees who were fired without cause that tested the limits of the president's power to fire federal officials.The Trump administration had argued that Article II of the Constitution gives the president unrestricted removal power, and said Congress could not limit the removal of federal prosecutors.But in his decision, Furman ruled that Comey's firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, a landmark law enacted in 1978 that provides protections for federal workers. The Trump administration, he wrote, is attempting to "upend" long-settled case law allowing Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers."Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system," Furman wrote.Comey had served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan since 2015, handling high-profile criminal cases against figures including Sean "Diddy" Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. national.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
national.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
national.body:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

national.title: Eric Bauza, modern voice of Bugs Bunny and other Looney Tunes characters, dies at 46
national.summary: Bauza's career gave voice to beloved Looney Tunes characters in "Puss in Boots," "Muppet Babies," "Avatar: The Last Airbender," and countless others.
national.body:
Eric Bauza, the award-winning voice actor whose performances of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more characters made him the modern voice of Looney Tunes, has died. He was 46.

Bauza died suddenly late Sunday, his family said in a statement. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner reported that he died at his home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease.

Beginning in 2001, Bauza amassed more than 400 voice acting credits in a career that gave voice to beloved characters in animated Looney Tunes series including "Puss in Boots," "Muppet Babies," "Avatar: The Last Airbender," and countless others. He won three Children's and Family Emmy Awards, from 2022 to 2025.

"Looney Tunes will always have a special place in my heart," Bauza said in an interview with The Associated Press this year. "I watched them on Saturday mornings originally. It's not just the voice but the overall aesthetic has influenced me as an artist."

Raised in Scarborough, Ontario by Filipino immigrant parents, Bauza found his passion for voice acting as a teenager. In high school, he would deliver the P.A. system morning announcements in various cartoon voices.

In voicing Looney Tunes characters, Bauza faithfully and reverentially channeled Mel Blanc. So great was his affection for Blanc that, in conversation, he would even toss out an impression of Blanc outside the recording booth. Bauza last year told The New York Times: "Mel Blanc is like the voice of God for me."

Bauza's Looney Tunes work included such feature films as "Space Jam: A New Legacy" (2021), "The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie" (2024) and this year's "Coyote vs. Acme." That film, in which Wile E. Coyote takes the Acme Corporation to court for its defective products, became a modest cause célèbre after Warner Bros. opted not to release it.

After an outcry from fans, partly stoked by Bauza, the film eventually found a distributor in Ketchup Entertainment and surpassed $100 million at the worldwide box office. While the film was in limbo, Bauza argued for its release at the 2024 Annie Awards, in the voice of Daffy Duck.

national.title: Delegations meet in Iran with the Middle East on edge over potential for renewed fighting
national.summary: Iran says diplomacy remains possible but rejects U.S. demands for surrender.
national.body:
CAIRO (AP) — High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said.

The talks came as many in Iran are anxious about a possible return to all-out war. Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats before elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

The war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also topics of the talks, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak with reporters.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security." Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said during the talks Monday that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries.

Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability."

Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the United States, as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran's nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks.

national.title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
national.summary: Two bishops in images that show them praying with Trump have said they believed the meeting was private.
national.body:
Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.

Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".

Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.

In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".

"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.

"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.

A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.

Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.

national.title: Police arrest teenager after shooting that injured 12, including children, in Florida
national.summary: The incident happened on Saturday night, close to an American football stadium where a game had just been played.
national.body:
Police have arrested a teenager in connection with a shooting on Saturday that injured 12 people in Florida.

The incident took place at 20:00 local time (01:00 Sunday GMT), close to an American football stadium in the city of Tallahassee where a university game had recently been played.

Eleven people were injured by gunfire, local police said, while another hurt their ankle while fleeing the scene. Six of the victims were children.

Anthony Rivers III, 15, has been charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.

Police said the shooting followed an altercation between people who knew each other and that additional arrests were possible.

None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, they said in a statement.

"What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said.

"We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy."

national.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around
national.summary: As polls pointed to defeat, millions joined a 'Lula's Army' channel that is credited with helping transform online enthusiasm into real-world mobilisation.
national.body:
A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.

Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.

At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.

Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.

Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.

For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.

national.title: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections
national.summary: Voters blame Trump, pointing to the Republican president's tariff policies and the war he started with Iran.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump would prefer that voters not worry about inflation . But it's hard for them to ignore.

Filling up a basic Ford F-150 truck now costs about $100, up $30 from a year ago. Mortgage rates have jumped to levels that have depressed home sales. And for the past 12 months, consumer prices have risen faster than paychecks, making the average family poorer.

One week before midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on his second term, Trump is struggling to deliver on his campaign promise to bring down costs, even as he insists the country has entered an economic "golden age." The same frustration that powered his comeback two years ago could now cost Republicans control of Congress.

"Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump insists while campaigning, vowing that interest rates and oil prices will plunge once the war with Iran — which he started — comes to an end.

The word "affordability," he says, is nothing but "a con job by the Democrats," adding that "it doesn't mean anything to anybody."

That rhetoric comes as voters say they're struggling to afford basics like fuel and groceries and as they blame Trump for higher costs, pointing to the Republican president's aggressive tariff policies and the ongoing, unpopular war with Iran.

Record-high diesel prices, in particular, have driven up shipping and farming costs, creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, where Democrats appear uniquely competitive in races that will shape Trump's final two years in office.

"The costs of things are absolutely the first thing people talk about, but also it's their pay not keeping up with the cost," said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. "It's a double whammy."

national.title: Notable Deaths in 2026
national.summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
national.body:
A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.

By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Actor Tom Skerritt (Aug. 25, 1933-Oct. 21, 2026) was an indelible presence in such films as "M*A*S*H," "Alien," "Top Gun" and "A River Runs Through It." He won an Emmy Award for the 1990s series "Picket Fences." A ruggedly handsome actor with an easy-going presence, the Detroit native had originally planned on working behind the camera, and attended UCLA film school. After watching "Citizen Kane," he determined that, if he wanted to write and direct well, he'd need to know how to act. Mentored by rising talents Robert Altman and Hal Ashby, he soon found himself in front of the camera.

Skerritt's roster of nearly 200 films and TV roles began in the early 1960s, with the World War II drama "War Hunt," which co-starred Robert Redford. He played an Army surgeon in Altman's "M*A*S*H," a motorcycle cop in Ashby's "Harold and Maude," the captain of a fated outer space tug in "Alien," a sheriff investigating murders on the Stephen King thriller "The Dead Zone," an instructor at the Navy's school for elite fighter pilots in "Top Gun," and a strict minister and father in "A River Runs Through It" (directed by Redford).

He received the National Board of Review's best supporting actor award as Shirley MacLaine's husband in "The Turning Point."

Even as he was landing starring roles in popular films like "Ice Castles" and "Alien," Skerritt was also making appearances on TV in shows like "Cannon," "Barnaby Jones" and "Baretta." He told The A/V Club in 2019 that his journeyman actor ethos was born of necessity: "I had to make a living, you know. You have to do what you have to do — I had three kids. I had to raise the kids myself, so it's a very delicate balance. … I never could imagine myself as a movie star because that's not what I wanted to do. ... I just wanted us to get by. I didn't want us to have to move into a trailer park camp because I couldn't afford any rent, you know?"

But his rough-hewn good looks and naturalistic talent made him a welcome addition to films like "Up in Smoke," "Steel Magnolias," "SpaceCamp," "The Rookie," "Contact," "Smoke Signals," and "Texas Rangers." He starred as small-town Sheriff Jimmy Brock in the 1990s series "Picket Fences," and played the patriarch of the Kennedy family in the TV series "Jackie Bouvier Kennedy Onassis." He also made appearances in "Cheers," "Chicago Hope," "Will & Grace," "The West Wing," "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit," "The Good Wife," and "Madam Secretary."

national.summary: Here's what to know about Starlink and Starshield, the technologies Ukraine is relying on in the war against Russia.
national.body: Over the past month, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. national.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
national.summary: A stretch of water in the west of the continent is now called the Amos Channel after the ex-BBC journalist.
national.body:
Part of Antarctica has been named after former BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos.

A stretch of water between Rothschild Island and Alexander Island in the west of the White Continent is now called the Amos Channel.

Amos was given the honour for his "exceptional and influential role in bringing Antarctic research to the forefront of public understanding" during his 38-year career at BBC News, the naming committee said.

The channel is a new feature in Antarctica that appeared when a chunk of ice that connected Rothschild and Alexander Islands disintegrated.

The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs , the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship , the Endurance.

"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.

Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.

"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.

national.summary: Americans are forecast to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, with the average consumer shelling out hundreds of dollars.
national.body: Americans are on track to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year amid rising costs associated with the national scarefest, according to the National Retail Federation. Consumers are forecast to shell out $4.1 billion on candy alone. Cocoa costs remain elevated despite surging over the last two years, with shipping and other expenses also pushing up treat costs. Despite higher prices, the NRF expects consumers to spend $400 million more on Halloween this year than in 2025, and $1.9 billion more than in 2024. A poll from consulting firm PwC found that the average person expects to spend about $263; parents often spend the most because they're shopping for multiple Halloween events. Two-thirds of Americans think Halloween has gotten too expensive, according to a recent survey from personal finance site WalletHub. Why costumes cost more this yearThe general manager of Chicago Costume, Cortland Hickey, told CBS News higher transportation and fulfillment costs are driving up Halloween-related prices this year."The tariff costs are pretty much baked into the products as opposed to being a surprise like they were last year," Hickey said. "But now it's the fuel surcharges and the cost of diesel and those kinds of things when you're receiving products on pallets and truckloads. "For shoppers ordering online, waiting until the last minute can mean paying more for rush shipping or risking a costume that arrives after Halloween. Online shopping is less popular for Halloween purchases this year, with 27% of consumers planning to shop online, slightly down from 31% in 2025, according to the National Retail Federation. Why candy is expensiveChocolate prices are expected to be 8% higher than last Halloween, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. FinanceBuzz found that a 100-piece bag of assorted Halloween candy costs an average of $16.96 in 2026, up 3.5% from last year and 71% higher than in 2021. Mondelez, the maker of Sour Patch Kids and Swedish Fish, raised prices on gummy candy packs 39%, while Ferrero, whose candy brands include Butterfinger, Crunch and Baby Ruth, raised chocolate pack prices nearly 19%. The higher prices are a lagging effect of the cocoa market. national.title: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
national.summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
national.body:
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.

The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."

national.title: Thousands of observers from the right and left will descend on polling places to monitor the vote on Election Day
national.summary: The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning.
national.body:
Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office.

They won't be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times.

The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy.

The Democratic National Committee created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes, said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC.

That's as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment.

On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign.

"We've never done this before," Kleeb said of the party's sweeping efforts. But "we've never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process."

national.title: Nurse killed in attack while responding to Ebola alert in DR Congo
national.summary: Local youths reportedly accused the health workers of contaminating water sources and spreading Ebola.
national.body:
A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.

In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days.

More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.

Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.

The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.

The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.

This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared.

national.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
national.summary: The AI company, which makes the popular Claude chatbot, has filed for an initial public offering that could be one of the biggest ever.
national.body:
Anthropic is taking a big step toward a blockbuster stock listing that would rank among the biggest IPOs ever. Patrick Sison/AP Photo hide caption

The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.

Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion .

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June . Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Understanding AI Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs call for AI development to slow down, OpenAI to delay IPO Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks .

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The NPR Politics Podcast How do you solve a problem like AI? The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice , with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

national.title: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
national.summary: The R&B star previously pleaded guilty to affray, after attacking a music producer with a glass bottle.
national.body:
US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.

The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.

Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".

The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.

The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."

CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.

national.summary: Prosecutors have indicted Devin Jacob Ballard for a killing that has caused outrage in Japan, local media reports.
national.body:
A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.

Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.

Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.

It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.

Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.

Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".

Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.

It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.

national.title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
national.summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
national.body:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.

Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".

Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.

In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.

Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.

The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.

Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.

national.title: Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate pauses midterms campaigning after car crash
national.summary: Mary Peltola, who suffered minor injuries, is running in one of the most closely watched races in the upcoming elections.
national.body:
Mary Peltola, Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, has paused campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections after sustaining "minor injuries" in a car crash.

Peltola, 53, and her family were travelling to an event on Saturday when the vehicle they were in was hit by another driver, her campaign said in a statement.

She is running in one of the most closely watched races in the elections, which take place on 3 November - one that could help decide the balance of power in government.

Peltola has rescheduled campaign events "as she takes time to recover" on the advice of medical professionals, her campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, said in a statement.

"Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," Bruce said.

Peltola is trying to unseat incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has classified the Alaska senate race as a "toss-up", meaning neither the Republicans nor the Democrats hold a decisive advantage.

Trump told the justice department to file a federal lawsuit last week to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.

The suit said the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.

national.title: Serbia's populist strongman Vucic outplayed all his opponents. Then the students came
national.summary: Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference.
national.body:
BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia's populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country's politics for 14 years. Then came the students.

The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students in a parliamentary election. The students had led protests for almost two years before unseating him in a historic change of government.

The 56-year-old political veteran easily outplayed political opponents in the past and thought he could do it again. Ahead of Sunday's ballot he pulled a maneuver in the style of his ally Russian President Vladimir Putin when he resigned the presidency to pursue a bid to become the prime minister.

Vucic then launched a fierce campaign involving favorable around-the-clock coverage on state media and attacks on opponents. He handed out cash to voters and promised higher pensions, new roads and cheaper medicines.

It didn't work. The diverse youth movement's message that rampant corruption, cronyism and organized crime under Vucic were eating away at the country resonated widely with voters.

The student protests first started in 2024 after a collapsed canopy at a renovated train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people, triggering claims that graft-fueled negligence led to poor construction work and eventually to the crash.

Defiant, Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference.

"I want people to know," he said. "This was the verification of a revolution that they carried out directly with support of different European countries and the deep American state, the one that is also against President (Donald) Trump."

national.title: Violent crime victimization fell 25% in 2025, DOJ survey shows
national.summary: A new preliminary survey finds that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25%, compared with 2024. The DOJ called it the largest decline since 1973.
national.body: A preliminary survey released on Monday found that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25% compared with the prior year, a significant drop that the Justice Department claimed represents the largest decline since 1973.The National Crime Victimization Survey, conducted by the Census Bureau and released by the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Statistics, found that there were an estimated 669,000 fewer violent crimes, excluding simple assaults, committed in 2025 compared with 2024.Aggravated assault victimization dropped an estimated 31%, with about 390,000 fewer incidents in 2025, compared with the prior year.The data for the survey comes from a sample of interviews in U.S. households of people who are 12 or older. The interviewees were asked questions about the frequency, characteristics and consequences of criminal victimization.The survey for 2025 consisted of 101,980 household interviews. Overall, 53% of eligible households completed interviews, the Bureau of Justice Statistics said.Other findings from the preliminary results of the survey showed that robbery was down 27% in 2025, property crime victimization was down 19%, burglary and trespassing were down 25% and motor vehicle theft was down 29%.The preliminary results from the survey bolster findings from earlier this year in the FBI's Uniform Crime Report, which showed that violent crime rates plummeted in 2025 with the country's murder rate reaching a 20-year low.That report, which compiles crime data from most law enforcement agencies across the nation, also recorded significant year-over-year decreases in multiple categories. Aggravated assaults fell by 7.2%, rapes declined by 7.6% and robbery was down about 18.5%.President Trump and his allies have sought to capitalize on the decrease in violent crime rates as they have campaigned across the country ahead of the midterms to try to help Republicans retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.In a break from prior traditions, the White House unveiled the findings from the FBI's Uniform Crime Report ahead of a campaign event on Long Island, New York, that was also attended by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel.

national.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner's human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
national.summary: Andre McKechnie, 55, is serving a life sentence for murder. He took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the court last year. He argued being refused Vegemite breached the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act.
national.body:
FILE - A piece of toast is prepared with Vegemite in Sydney, Australia, Monday, Nov. 17, 2025. Rick Rycroft/AP hide caption

MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state's ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian."

Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.

He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to "enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background," court documents showed.

Breakfast Around the World In Australia, Vegemite is a breakfast staple at the center of an unusual court case Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities' refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite "limited his cultural rights" under the charter.

But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities' goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.

"The limitation on Mr. McKechnie's ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner," Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.

Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state's 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs' ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.

local.title: State judicial commission admonishes Ontario County Judge Karle
local.summary: Admonishment is the second-lowest punishment the commission administers in cases of misconduct.
local.body:
Ontario County Judge Kristina Karle has been admonished by the state Commission on Judicial Conduct for allegedly trying to influence a case being handled by another judge.

Admonishment is the second-lowest punishment the commission administers in cases of misconduct. Karle presides over county and family court, and is an acting state Supreme Court justice.

The case concerned the daughter of a friend of Karle's sister, according to the commission's determination. Records show Karle reached out to the judge and requested "if legally permissible" that the judge set bail for the daughter to keep her from being released.

Karle added in a text message to that judge that the defendant had "severe drug addiction," that her weight was down to "like 76 pounds," that she had frostbite from living under a bridge, and that she was being sexually assaulted on the streets, the determination said.

"Her family feels this may be the last chance to save her," read part of the text message. "She always runs – even from hospitals. We just want to save her life and get her dried out and potentially in to treatment if possible," the text message read.

The judge sought legal advice regarding the request and ultimately reported it to the commission and recused themselves from the case. The determination does not identify the judge.

Karle also reported herself after the judge indicated they weren't comfortable with the request. The commission said she cooperated throughout the matter.

"In accepting the jointly recommended sanction of admonition, we have taken into consideration that respondent has acknowledged that her conduct was improper and warrants public discipline," the determination concluded. "Respondent immediately apologized to the other judge and self-reported her conduct to the Commission. We trust that respondent has learned from this experience and in the future will act in strict accordance with her obligation to abide by all the Rules Governing Judicial Conduct."

local.title: Open house set for Wednesday on Olmsted bridges study
local.summary: Monroe County initiated the study last year to assess the conditions of the three bridges and develop recommendations for their short- and long-term maintenance.
local.body:
Monroe County, the city of Rochester, and the Genesee Transportation Council are holding an informational open house Wednesday on their study of the three Olmsted pedestrian bridges in Genesee Valley Park.

The county initiated the study last year and hired the council to draft it. The study is assessing the conditions of the bridges and developing recommendations for their short- and long-term maintenance.

Local News Genesee Valley Park has three Olmsted-designed bridges. Monroe County wants to know what it would take to restore them Jeremy Moule The county wants to contract with Genesee Transportation Council to develop a restoration plan for the arched bridges. The open house is from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Genesee Waterways Center, 149 Elmwood Ave. An optional walking tour of the westernmost bridge begins at 5 p.m.

The bridges were not part of Frederick Law Olmsted's original design for the park. They were designed by the Olmsted Brothers firm and added to the park between 1916 and 1919 to help reconnect trails that were disrupted when the canal was brought through the park.

The reinforced concrete bridges are safe to use but have been deteriorating.

A water conservation order for the village continued Monday — the week after water system director Luis Fred told of
local.body:
Two weeks of sunshine is evidently troubling the Fredonia water treatment plant and reservoir. There's a dark cloud there, anyway, due to a snag in a chlorination improvement project.

A water conservation order for the village continued Monday -- the week after water system director Luis Fred told officials that one of his new chlorination pumps is already broken.

"We remain under a temporary Water Conservation due to the severe lack of rain," Fredonia's official social media page posted early Monday morning. The page is controlled by Mayor Michael Ferguson.

The post reminded that Fredonia water customers can conserve by only doing full loads of laundry and dishes; keeping showers shorter; and keeping away from watering lawns or washing cars.

"Working together we can get through this," the post concluded.

Fredonia's Office of Emergency Management made a similar social media post about the continuing water conservation order on Monday morning.

Looming in the background is an equipment problem that clearly irked village officials when they learned about it last week.

Fred told them at a Board of Trustees workshop that a pump which transfers chlorine from a storage tank "had a problem... We ended up having to buy a new pump. It should be here this week. It was supposed to be here today but didn't come. Chemicals are still in abundance due to storage."

local.title: Hyatt awaits $16M overhaul as other hotels face uncertain future
local.summary: The Riverside and former Wyndham once accounted for nearly half of all downtown hotel rooms. Now one has been ransacked, and the other is wrapped in corrugated steel.
local.body:
A $16 million renovation meant to elevate the downtown Hyatt Regency to a top-flight, full-service hotel will begin "as soon as possible," officials say.

"Our goal is to make it shine again, you know?" said Hyatt general manager Jay Rettberg. "Be that exclamation point."

In a downtown looking to regain its pre-pandemic momentum, the project is a bright spot. The Hyatt has been a critical piece of local travel and tourism. Now it is an anchor in a hotel scene otherwise in flux. It is the largest hotel in the Center City since the Rochester Riverside closed in 2020. The Wyndham was the next largest until it, too, shut down this summer.

"For a city of our size with a population of our size, you know we're short about 1,000 hotel rooms from what we would ideally have," Deputy Mayor Michael Burns said. "And so, the rooms at the Hyatt are critical — as are the rooms over at the former Wyndham Hotel."

The Riverside and former Wyndham accounted for nearly half, almost 700, of all downtown hotel rooms. A lack of hotel capacity, made worse by the closures, has cost the city nearly $50 million in lost meeting business since 2022, according to VisitRochester estimates. And the buildings have become a blight in the heart of downtown — one ransacked , the other wrapped in corrugated steel to head off a similar plight.

local.title: New hires at Lollypop Farm signal the return of vital services for pets and local rescues
local.summary: Staffing shortages this summer temporarily halted spay/neuter surgeries. Three full-time veterinarians were recently hired following a national search.
local.body:
A veterinarian shortage in the U.S. has for years presented challenges to pet owners and rescue groups seeking care for their companion animals.

Even the Rochester region's largest animal welfare organization is not immune to its effects.

In June, Lollypop Farm, the Humane Society of Greater Rochester, temporarily paused spay/neuter surgeries for pets in the care of community rescue organizations due to staff shortages.

This week, Lollypop announced the recent hiring of three veterinarians to close that gap.

"We were recruiting nationally. We did have a search firm helping us out, but ultimately we succeeded most with people who were familiar with the area and had a true passion for shelter medicine," said vice president and COO Adrienne McHargue.

Now, with a total of four full-time staff veterinarians, part-time medical director, and 10 veterinary technicians, as well as the recent addition of veterinarians who helped on a per diem basis during the summer, Lollypop hopes to provide the same level of community service it did in 2024. McHargue said that is when they began losing veterinarians through relocation and discovered it was challenging to find replacements.

As the organization grows its capacity to provide veterinary care, it will be reopening its S.N.I.P program in November. The program allows income eligible pet owners to apply for spay/neuter services for their pets at a reduced cost. Lollypop also expects to improve access to veterinary services for partner rescue organizations in the community, including vaccination clinics, wellness exams, and sterilization surgeries.

A new mobile veterinary clinic is expected to launch in the near future, bringing wellness services directly to underserved communities where transportation may be a barrier for pet owners.

local.title: Both parties see opportunities to make gains in NY Senate
local.summary: Republicans are trying to reduce Democrats’ 41-22 state Senate majority while Democrats are trying to grow it.
local.body:
Early voting has begun for this year’s general election, and every seat in the New York state Legislature is on the ballot.

In the state Senate, Republicans are trying to reduce Democrats’ 41-22 majority while Democrats are trying to grow it.

One race where Democrats see opportunity is the 43rd district, which covers Rensselaer County and parts of Albany and Washington counties. The seat has been long held by Republicans, including former Senate Majority Leader Joe Bruno, but the latest redistricting gives Democrats and unaffiliated voters a registration edge.

Enter Devin Lander , state historian and first-time candidate, who is vying to unseat the district’s incumbent Republican Sen. Jake Ashby .

“I think it's very important symbolically,” Lander said, though noting that the district has changed. “The enrollments are different now. People's expectations are different now. And I think, you know, people are … ready for new leadership.”

“It's a purple district,” Ashby said. "And I think that I represent that, and I have very well ... during my time in the Assembly, and also in the Senate."

Ashby served one term in the Assembly before being elected to the Senate in 2022.

There also are contested seats on Long Island, as well as in the Hudson Valley, the Capital Region and Central New York. Both parties are trying to reach voters contending with the rising cost of living and high energy bills.

local.title: Assemblywoman proposes tighter limits on screens in schools
local.summary: The reaction was swift earlier this year when the Salamanca City Central School District proposed using a Realbotix educational robot and digital avatar designed to support teaching and learning in its high school STEAM program. That project was quickly shelved after widespread criticism, but a stat
local.body:
The reaction was swift earlier this year when the Salamanca City Central School District proposed using a Realbotix educational robot and digital avatar designed to support teaching and learning in its high school STEAM program.

That project was quickly shelved after widespread criticism, but a state lawmaker wants to go a step further by implementing grade-based limits on students' access to internet-enabled devices. Assemblywoman Sarahana Shrestha, D-Kingston, recently introduced the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use Of Screens (FOCUS) Act. The bill (A.11669) would phase in grade-based limits on pupils’ access to Internet-enabled devices and limit the use of social media, gaming, direct messaging, and other apps Shrestha said serve little to no instructional purpose. The legislation would constitute a major change for schools in the state. The earliest it could be discussed is the next state legislative session starting in January.

"Known as the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens (FOCUS) Act, this bill aligns with the precedent set by New York’s 2025 bell-to-bell ban for students’ personal devices, which put an end to the havoc that smartphones were wreaking in classrooms through their ability to addict, distract, and impair the mental health of student users," Shrestha wrote in her legislative justification. "The FOCUS Act builds upon this framework by recognizing that it makes little sense for the State of New York to go through the trouble of limiting personal devices if we are then going to bring them right back in the form of school-issued devices."

For early childhood and elementary school pupils in pre-kindergarten through fifth grades, Shrestha proposes students generally be prohibited from accessing screens and instead complete assignments via pencil and paper wherever feasible. For middle school students in sixth through eighth grades, students will access screens via a computer cart or lab model wherein devices are rotated amongst students in a classroom. High school students would access screens as part of a cart model or on a one-to-one basis with caregiver opt in,

Shrestha also proposes creating a right to analog learning, meaning schools and teachers would prioritize in-class and homework assignments that allow students to complete them in a screen-free manner wherever feasible. Parents and students would additionally be able to opt out of screens where a reasonable non-digital alternative to completing an assignment exists, and schools would be prohibited from retaliating against pupils who exercise this right, The opt-out provision would not apply to assignments where use of the technology is inherent to the learning objective of the assignment, such as assignments undertaken pursuant to the state Education Department's computer science and digital fluency standards.

SAINT-DENIS, France (AP) -- Aaron Rodgers threw one touchdown pass and Chris Boswell kicked three field goals in Pittsburgh’s 16-10 win over the New Orleans Saints on Sunday in the NFL’s first regular-season game in France.

Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards and Rodgers completed 19 of 30 passes for 212 yards and scrambled for a key first down late in fourth quarter as the Steelers (5-2) won their third straight game.

Linebacker Payton Wilson had a red zone interception of Tyler Shough in the third quarter and the Saints (2-5) couldn’t recover. New Orleans rushed for just 18 yards.

With the Saints threatening on their opening drive of the second half, Wilson stepped in front of a short pass intended for Chris Olave. The Steelers got in field-goal position and Boswell was good from 39 yards for a 16-10 lead.

CHARLOTTE, N.C. (AP) -- Bucky Irving ran for 106 yards and two touchdowns, and Tampa Bay forced four turnovers as the Buccaneers hammered Carolina in Baker Mayfield’s return.

Mayfield, who missed the previous three games with a dislocated right thumb, attempted just 11 passes and threw for 64 yards while wearing a protective glove on his right hand. That was more than enough for him to improve to 7-1 against the Panthers, including 6-1 since joining the Bucs (2-5).

Mayfield didn’t need to do much because Tampa Bay’s run game, defense and special teams dominated. The Bucs had 258 yards on the ground, with Sean Tucker adding a 46-yard touchdown run to put Tampa Bay up by 37.

Carolina’s Bryce Young turned the ball over three times. Al-Quadin Muhammad had a strip-sack of Young that Calijah Kancey returned 32 yards for a touchdown.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, a new
local.body:
On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill/Working Families Tax Cuts Act into law, and it’s unfortunate that very few parents know this legislation provides the largest national expansion of K-12 education freedom in our nation’s history.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, a new federal Education Freedom Tax Credit provides up to $1,700 per individual (up to $3,400 for married couples filing jointly) for qualified cash contributions to a Scholarship Granting Organization. Yet as with most bills passed out of our Congress, there are regulations and deadlines.

On Oct. 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service released proposed regulations for the credit’s 2027 launch, making the new credit accessible to families and providing administrative guidance for taxpayers, states and SGOs while protecting scholarship funds from fraud and abuse.

SGOs can use contributions from individuals to provide scholarships to students for a range of education-related expenses incurred in connection with a K-12 public, private (including religious) or charter school. This can include tuition for students to attend a school of choice, tutoring for students attending a public school, special education services for students with disabilities, books, supplies and extended day programs.

Why is not this great education freedom opportunity in the headlines during such a consequential midterms election year?

Students from a household whose prior-year income is up to 300% of the area’s median gross income, adjusted for family size, may qualify for a scholarship through the Education Freedom Tax Credit. Our Treasury Department estimates that about 95% of American children live in households that may qualify for such a scholarship.

One challenge for parents in certain states to access these great benefits is that due to an absurd interpretation of U.S. Senate rules by the Senate parliamentarian, senators inserted a state “opt-in” condition for taxpayers in those states to claim the federal credit for contributions to SGOs in their home state.

Yet Treasury reports that as of Sept. 14, 2026, only 30 states have elected to identify SGOs in their state that will be eligible to receive contributions from individuals utilizing the Education Freedom Tax Credit.

entertainment.title: Walter Koenig, the Russian Crewman Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
entertainment.summary: He joined the TV series for the second season but had more to do on another acclaimed sci-fi program, 'Babylon 5.'
entertainment.body:
Walter Koenig, the boyish actor who remains an integral part of Star Trek lore thanks to his portrayal of the Russian crewman Pavel Chekov, has died. He was 90.

Koenig, also known for playing the scoundrel Alfred Bester on another sci-fi space series, Warner Bros. Television’s Babylon 5 , died Sunday of natural causes in his home in North Hollywood, his rep announced.

Raised in Manhattan as a son of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig joined Gene Roddenberry’s Star Trek for the start of its second season and appeared on 36 of the 50 episodes that aired in 1967-68 and 1968-69. He also portrayed Pavel Andreievich Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies, released from 1979 through 1991, that emanated from the NBC show. Related Stories Movies Eric Bauza, the Modern Voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Other Iconic Characters, Dies at 46 TV Peggy King, Singer and 'George Gobel Show' Star of Television's Golden Age, Dies at 96

In a 2013 interview for the TV Academy Foundation, Koenig said he didn’t watch Star Trek before he came aboard. “I’d flip through the channels and I’d see Styrofoam rocks — they were so obviously Styrofoam — and I said, ‘This has got to be phony.’ I didn’t give it a chance,” he recalled.

The actor portrayed a Russian for the first time in his career — a student who had defected to the U.S. — on a 1963 episode of the NBC drama Mr. Novak .

He then guest-starred as a young sergeant whose goal of being promoted to officer is complicated by the fact that his mother is a communist on a 1964 installment of The Lieutenant , another series created by Roddenberry.

After his Star Trek audition, Koenig spent a couple of lonely hours in an outer office wondering if he had gotten the job when he was approached by a man and asked to follow him into the wardrobe room.

“He drops on his knees in front of me,” Koenig said, “and takes my crotch in his hand, and I’m saying, ‘What are you doing?!” I didn’t see the tape-measuring ruler in his other hand, and he was measuring from my crotch to my cuff to decide how long my pants should be. He says, ‘You do have to have a costume, don’t you?’

entertainment.title: Sam Fender Criticizes Own Tour Prices, Eliminates Premium Standing Tickets for U.K. Shows: ‘It’s Bollocks’
entertainment.summary: "I’m not happy with these prices, they’re getting changed," he wrote.
entertainment.body:
Sam Fender is heading out on a Proper Massive stadium tour in June 2027, but he’s “not happy” with the prices of his own shows.

The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram Saturday (Oct. 24) that he was disappointed with the pricing for the upcoming run and that “they’re getting changed.” Fender is due to play a number of stadium shows in Newcastle, Manchester, Cardiff, Edinburgh and two nights at London’s Wembley Stadium in June.

Fender first responded to the tour prices in an Instagram comment writing, “I’m not happy with these prices, they’re getting changed. It got inflated well more than I’d had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on.”

The “Rein Me In” star responded to criticism of a premium — and more expensive — ticket for the front standing area. “The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it,” he explained. “I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs. It’s bollocks and it won’t be happening on this tour.”

Fender revealed the revised prices on his Instagram Story Sunday and changed the layout of the shows. “I’ve managed to get front standing tickets removed from the U.K. stadium tour. Whoever buys a standing ticket gets as much chance as anyone to be at the front. No more 120 quid standing tickets either.”

He added, “Costs are astronomical compared to two years ago, I can’t control the venue and ticketing fees, that’s a sad reality of today’s industry.”

General admission tickets will now begin at £85 ($113), with seated tickets priced at £55 ($73), £75 ($100) and £95 ($126) depending on the seats’ locations. These prices exclude venue and ticket company fees, and the £1 per ticket contribution to the LIVE Trust which supports grassroots venues across the U.K.

A presale for tickets begins at 9:30 GMT on Wednesday (Oct. 28), followed by a general sale on Friday (Oct. 31).

entertainment.title: ‘Donnie Darko’: THR’s 2001 Review
entertainment.summary: On October 26, 2001, writer-director Richard Kelly's feature opened in theaters after its Sundance premiere.
entertainment.body:
On October 26, 2001, writer-director Richard Kelly’s Donnie Darko opened in theaters following its Sundance Film Festival bow early in the year. The feature, starring Jake Gyllenhaal and Jena Malone, made just over $8 million globally. The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below:

Quick: What rhymes with “Darko”? “Bizarro,” “sicko,” “weirdo,” “nutso.” You get the idea of this film real fast from the tide, which is the good and bad news. Playing in the dramatic competition at this year’s Sundance Film Festival, Donnie Darko is the latest progeny of the alienated, upper-middle-class, private school-kid genre. In its dark depiction of the well-manicured suburbs, one feels the dark shadow of Kevin Spacey and a bouquet of dead roses hovering over this odd and bright offspring.

With its mix of teenage alienation, anti-authority diatribes and heaps of personality disorder, Darko is appealing in a kind of neo- Heathers , anti-establishment way. With blistering satirical slants and a steady mix of acidic jabs at middle-class life, Darko should be boffo among the teen and young adults segment as well as those viewers still plugged into a sophomoric self-identity.

A mixed bag genetically and qualitatively, Darko gyrates around the brooding downward spiral of its titular character, fusing together black comedy, paranormal activity and teenage angst. Ultimately, filmmaker Richard Kelly’s narrative bursts fizzle into a confusing meltdown, but along the way, it’s stoked with enough wiggy comedy and incendiary situations to keep its target teen audience straight up and satisfied. At its Sundance screening, there wasn’t merely a generation gap between the twentysomethings and elder thirtysomethings but more of a generational abyss as pockets howled with glee while others sat in stony, seen-it-before silence.

In this dare-to-be-wicked romp, dark-coiffed boy of privilege Donnie Darko meanders about in a medicated glaze. He’s bright (high Iowa test scores), talented and baffling to everyone: parents, teachers, friends and siblings. Donnie is a bit of a cherubic-looking Edward Scissorhands who, on one of his less sullen days, comes across as a charming, intriguing kid. But Donnie is terminally dark-sided: He is torment ed by the oafishness of his peers, the well-meaning obtuseness of his parents and the dunderheaded ways of his supposed role models. And all these burdens do not make him happy, nor does the fuddle in his head caused by the prescription pills he takes for what seems to be a paranoid/schizophrenic disorder give him any consistent focus in life.

entertainment.title: Turnstile Bring Hardcore Fury (and 60,000 Fans) to Washington Monument: Exclusive Photos
entertainment.summary: The group's fans descended on the nation's capital over the weekend for a human rights fundraiser in the shadow of the Washington monument.
entertainment.body:
Turnstile brought the pit to America’s front yard on Saturday (Oct. 24), playing a free show for more than 60,000 fans gathered near the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. The Baltimore hardcore group’s biggest show to date was also the final gig on the North American tour in support of their Never Enough album and a landmark for the group whose Maryland-bred singer is a practical native of the nation’s capital.

The show, “Turnstile at the Washington Monument,” was co-hosted by Human Concern International and aimed at raising funds to benefit humanitarian efforts in Palestine, Sudan and Lebanon.

The gig drew legions of the Grammy-winning hardcore band’s fans to the hilly lawn near the iconic monument for a rager that featured massive, roiling mosh pits , a likely first for the august site that in the past has hosted everything from the massive 1963 civil rights March on Washington to this past summer’s tepid Great American State Fair Kickoff.

According to The Washington Post , singer Brendan Yates told the crowd, “Today we’re here to gather around music to celebrate humanity. But also to fight for it. Be loud enough for the White House to hear,” then leading the crowd in a pro-Palestinian chant, “Free Palestine!,” with his head turned toward the White House just blocks away, as well as “Free Sudan!” and “Free Lebanon!”

Before the 75-minute show, Human Concern International’s global director announced that the show had reportedly earned $150,000, easily surpassing the initial $100K goal. The 19-track setlist included such beloved songs as “Birds,” “Endless,” “Keep It Moving,” “Holiday,” “Blackout” and the finale, “T.L.C. (Turnstile Love Connection).”

Turnstile won their first of two Grammy Awards in February for best rock album ( Never Enough ) and best metal performance (“Birds”) and then made their Saturday Night Live debut earlier this month, becoming the first hardcore group to rock the Studio 8H stage since Fear’s legendarily chaotic 1981 debut.

entertainment.title: Layoffs Are Reshaping the Music Industry. jump.global Wants to Train Executives for What’s Next
entertainment.summary: Nick Maiale, executive coach and founder of jump.global, talks about his upcoming summit and why everyone should be in “the business of your first and last name."
entertainment.body:
The fourth annual jump.global summit in Los Angeles is just weeks away, on Nov. 8-10, and its founder, Nick Maiale , is convinced its timing couldn’t be more necessary. In the past month, Universal Music Group made significant cuts to its staff at record labels like MCA, Def Jam Records, Republic Records, Capitol Records and more — a continuation of its layoffs, which kicked off back in 2024. Still, Universal is far from the only music company culling employees this year.

“We need to dive into the fact that layoffs have become common in this industry,” Maiale tells Billboard. At the jump.global summit, which focuses on executive development, mental health and leadership skills for music professionals, Maiale preaches the gospel that every modern careerist should be in the “business of your first and last name.” At the conference, his name tags are just that — name tags. No company names and no titles are listed to create a level playing field.

Instead, he wants attendees to be focused on getting to know each other on a human level. Even his panelists, some of whom bear impressively high ranking titles at major companies, don’t tout their credentials either. Every speaker is vaguely listed on the jump.global website as simply a “music business human.”

Those who attend the three-day affair, which is part conference and part leadership retreat, are treated to a mix of small group break outs and panels, featuring names like Janelle Lopez Genzink, Stephen Brower, Jason Feinberg, Lexi Todd and Moody Jones. And while the summit has always been known to hand out free badges for people who have newly been laid off as a courtesy, Maiale says that, due to increased demand for these comped badges, he’s now upping the supply. This year, he estimates that 30% of attendees are laid-off employees looking for their next move. The other 70% are a mix of folks sent by their companies, folks who buy badges themselves and executive coaches.

While Maiale is going to address layoffs and how work in the music industry is changing at the conference, he clarifies: “the conference is definitely not a place where people come simply to complain about how the music industry is doing. What we want to do is be solutions-focused and opportunity-focused.”

I have heard you say many times with jump.global, that you’re promoting “the business of your first and last name.” Is that a mentality you have always had while working in music, or is it something that has developed more recently, in light of how much the music industry is changing and how uncertain it has become?

entertainment.body:
Logo text Look(smaxx) here: We finally have actual information on that rumored Clavicular Hulu documentary.

The Hollywood Reporter can first reveal that all that beef between the 20-year-old looksmaxxer, whose real name is Braden Peters, and Disney has resulted in a three-part true crime documentary series titled Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death . The Hulu doc is not and was never a documentary about Peters, rather it was about the dangerous and competitive worlds of looksmaxxing and social media; Peters just happens to be the most famous individual on that scene and his likeness is only used briefly. Specifically, the docuseries is about a mysterious death in Thailand (that has nothing whatsoever to do with Clavicular).

But since it’s been a while, the backstory: Peters served Disney/Hulu a cease and desist letter after he says he caught documentarians Jennings Brown and James Kristofik filming him backstage at the Elena Velez fashion show in February New York City without permission. Peters did not like that, but the encounter would be far from his biggest legal case this year.

Just last week, Peters pleaded not guilty to raping an underage girl after she was given alcohol while appearing on his livestream in 2025. In September, Peters was charged with two felony counts, one for rape and another for drugging a person for sexual intercourse. He also faces a misdemeanor count for providing alcohol to someone younger than 21.

Peters has denied the allegations, saying that the encounter was consensual. He has posted a video to his social media accounts showing screenshots of a text conversation and a photo of a handwritten letter, which were intercut over footage of Peters, shirtless and fixing his hair at an urban inner harbor. Beneath the posts, he’s written, “Theres better ways to make money then suing someone because they don’t want you,” and “Yeah still texting me to this day… totally not just trying to be greedy and get a check.”

“Deep in the manosphere, an underground movement promises to unlock human potential — bulging muscles, bigger penises, eternal youth. At its center is Dr. Tony Huge, a guru pushing homemade biohacks on a devoted following willing to risk everything for the cause,” the logline reads. “When Leo & Longevity, a penis-enlargement expert and one of Tony’s closest allies, is found dead in Thailand, alpha-male influencers become online sleuths, running wild with theories and questioning Tony Huge and his right-hand man, Connor Murphy. Soon, a darker pattern emerges: Leo isn’t the first of the inner circle to die under mysterious circumstances. entertainment.body:
Logo text Robert Pattinson is sounding off about Steven Soderbergh stepping up to help finish filming The Batman Part II .

Earlier this month, Soderbergh agreed to take the on-set directing reins for the DC Studios production in London after Matt Reeves had to step aside due to a personal family matter back in Los Angeles. Reeves remains involved in the production.

“I am so happy he’s come on to help Matt,” Pattinson told Games Radar during a recent interview while promoting the actor’s film Primetime . “It’s incredibly generous of him – and he’s doing it in the loveliest way. It’s completely selfless.” Related Stories Movies Lance Oppenheim Bribed Robert Pattinson With 200 Zyn Canisters to Star in 'Primetime' Movies 'The Batman Part II': Steven Soderbergh to Work with Matt Reeves to Complete Filming

Continued Pattinson: “I think Matt had put so much work into the script, and we’re almost done. So for someone to come in and say, ‘I just want to help Matt do it; I want to do it in conjunction with him and just get it to the edit.’ And to have someone who’s as talented as Steven doing it is great.”

As previously reported, the plan is for Soderbergh to work in London, while Reeves operates out of Los Angeles. Reeves will also be hands-on during the movie’s post-production in L.A. The film is said to be about two-thirds done.

“I thought Matt Reeves’ work on The Batman was stunning; it was intentional, specific, and rigorously coherent,” Soderbergh said in a statement. “The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.”

Added Reeves on social media: “Just to be clear, I am not leaving The Batman Part II . I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes.”

Pattinson is having a rather incredible year, having appeared in three successful films — The Drama , The Odyssey and Primetime , with Dune: Part Three still to come in December.
